lesson.title: Inflection Points: Where the Curve Changes Its Mind
lesson.summary: An inflection point is a location where concavity genuinely flips, from concave up to concave down or the reverse, and finding a place where f'' equals zero is only a candidate; confirming the point requires checking that the sign of f'' truly changes there rather than just touching zero.
lesson.body:
A point (c, f(c)) is called an inflection point if f is continuous at c and the concavity of f actually changes there, concave up on one side and concave down on the other, or the reverse. Finding candidates is easy: solve f''(x) = 0, or note any point where f'' is undefined but f itself is still continuous. But a candidate is not automatically the real thing. This is exactly the crossing versus touching distinction from the sign change analysis section: a zero of f'' produced by an odd power factor crosses through zero and gives a genuine inflection point, while a zero produced by an even power factor only touches zero, no sign change, and no inflection point at all. Skipping this check is the single most common mistake made when hunting for inflection points.

Return to f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5, with f''(x) = 6x - 6 = 6(x - 1). The only zero is x = 1, and (x - 1) appears to the first power, an odd power, so the sign genuinely changes there. This matches what was already found in the concavity sections: f'' is negative, concave down, on (negative infinity, 1), and positive, concave up, on (1, positive infinity). Since the sign truly flips at x = 1, it is a genuine inflection point. Its y-coordinate is f(1) = 1 - 3 - 9 + 5 = -6, so the inflection point is located at (1, -6).

Contrast that with g(x) = x^4 from the Second Derivative Test section, where g''(x) = 12x^2 also equals zero at x = 0. But 12x^2 is never negative, it is zero only at that single point and positive everywhere else, so there is no sign change at all, and x = 0 is not an inflection point, consistent with the earlier finding that x = 0 is actually a local minimum of x^4. f''(c) = 0 is necessary for an inflection point at c, when f'' exists there, but it is never sufficient on its own.

An inflection point can also occur where f'' fails to exist, as long as f itself stays continuous there. For f(x) = x^(1/3), the second derivative f''(x) = -(2/9) x^(-5/3) is undefined at x = 0, yet it can be shown that f'' is positive for x less than 0 and negative for x greater than 0, a genuine sign change, so x = 0 is an inflection point of x^(1/3) even though the graph has a vertical tangent line there rather than a flat one. The lesson is the same one repeated throughout this chapter sequence: it is always the sign change that certifies an inflection point, never the mere presence or absence of a derivative value.
